summary.summary: Hammersmith and Fulham borrowed a further £35m from the PWLB and repaid £16m in 2024/25, lifting debt from £269.2m to £288.3m (all fixed rate, average 3.75%), with 82.4% of the debt serviced by the housing account. The striking move is on the other side of the balance sheet: cash invested fell 72% in the year, from £159.3m to £44.2m, all now held short-term in money market funds and one £10m local-authority deposit. The total CFR rose from £614m to £766.7m, so the council is heavily under-borrowed (HRA internal borrowing alone is £222m) and future capital spend implies substantial further borrowing. All prudential indicators were met, with only 2% of debt maturing within 12 months, and the figures remain subject to external audit.

signals.headline: Debt up £19.1m to £288.3m in 2024/25 (£35m new PWLB less £16m repaid) while total CFR rose £152.7m to £766.7m
signals.why: The gap between a £767m borrowing need and £288m actual debt is a pipeline of future borrowing at today's higher rates.

signals.headline: Cash invested fell from £159.3m to £44.2m during 2024/25, all short-term, against £288.3m debt and £235m in-year capital spend
signals.why: A £115m cash rundown in one year leaves a thin buffer and points to external borrowing or further drawdown ahead.

news_drafts.headline: Hammersmith and Fulham schools-funding deficit reached £7.882m, forecast £17.5m by March 2027
news_drafts.lead:
Hammersmith and Fulham's deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) rose to £7.882m at the end of 2025/26 and is forecast to reach £17.5m by 31 March 2027, a rise of £9.618m. The council's annual audit report, put to its Audit Committee on 24 September, attributes this mainly to increased demand in high needs (the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities).

The council says it is eligible for the government's High Needs Stability Grant, which supports up to 90% of such deficits. Expected grant totals £16.237m, leaving the council to fund £1.263m from a reserve set up for the purpose. That depends on the Department for Education approving the council's Local SEND (special educational needs and disabilities) Reform Plan, which the council submitted by the deadline. Approval is pending. The council's risk report records the same position: if the plan is approved, 90% of the deficit will be funded through the grant.

The council's statement of accounts (its formal annual accounts) says that, in common with other London boroughs, high needs spending "has been significantly higher than the funding provided by central government". Separately, the risk report says the council achieved the highest available rating in its recent SEND inspection.

findings.headline: HRA capital programme reduced by £20.4m following review and rebalancing of housing investment
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account capital programme has been reduced by £20.401m, primarily from reductions in planned asset management works. This represents a rebalancing following review of what the HRA can afford, reducing the four-year HRA programme from £352.346m to £331.945m.
findings.matters: HRA reductions may reflect constraints on housing investment funding or reprioritisation, which affects the pace of building maintenance, fire safety compliance, and delivery of new affordable housing.
findings.figures: HRA reduction: £20.401m; Four-year HRA programme: £331.945m (revised from £352.346m); Housing component: £240.505m forecast
findings.quote: Reductions in planned spend relate to the ongoing review and rebalancing of the capital programme

findings.headline: VAT partial exemption breach would cost council £3m annually and poses material financial risk
findings.detail: The council's VAT partial exemption position faces breach risk from capital projects. Officers are actively managing significant projects to mitigate this risk. A breach of the partial exemption threshold would cost £3m per annum while the breach persists.
findings.matters: A £3m annual VAT cost is material to the council's financial position and capital programme sustainability; ongoing monitoring is required.
findings.figures: Potential VAT breach cost: £3m per annum
findings.quote: A breach would likely cost the Council £3m per year whilst in breach.

findings.headline: Council approving new borrowing of £1.24m for parking CCTV and £0.249m for business intelligence infrastructure
findings.detail: The council is requesting additional borrowing for two specific purposes: £1.2m for parking signage and CCTV facilities generating £0.275m annual revenue costs (MRP plus interest), funded from parking revenue; and £0.249m for business intelligence infrastructure generating £0.07m annual costs. These new borrowings increase the Capital Financing Requirement and create ongoing revenue pressures.
findings.matters: New borrowing approvals increase debt servicing costs in the revenue budget during a period of financial constraint, and demonstrate continued reliance on borrowing for operational infrastructure.
findings.figures: Parking schemes: £1.2m borrowing, £0.275m annual cost; Business Intelligence: £0.249m borrowing, £0.07m annual cost
findings.quote: Additional budget of £1.2m funded by borrowing is sought to provide signage and CCTV facilities throughout the borough. This will result in estimated £0.275m per year of additional revenue costs (MRP plus interest) which will be met from parking revenue budgets.

findings.headline: Civic Campus project experiencing continued delays pending outstanding HSE report on site incident
findings.detail: The Health & Safety Executive report on a site incident remains outstanding, delaying conclusion of the associated insurance claim. The Client Management Team has been expanded to include additional specialist technical and legal advisers to manage the project. This is a significant regeneration initiative involving the iconic town hall reopening.
findings.matters: Major capital projects with HSE involvement and incident investigations carry cost and schedule risks; outstanding insurance claim conclusions may affect financial position.
findings.figures: Civic Campus forecast 2026/27 spend: Hammersmith Town Hall Refurbishment £17.397m, Commercial Units Works £2.580m, Cinema Fit Out £2.250m
findings.quote: The Health & Safety Executive (HSE) report on the site incident is still awaited, and the Council is making representations to the HSE regarding this continued delay and its impact on the conclusion of the outstanding insurance claim.

findings.headline: Capital receipts forecast at £35.297m over four years faces risks from lower sales volumes and declining Right to Buy sales
findings.detail: The council's capital programme depends on receipts from housing development sales and Right to Buy purchases, approved when market conditions were stronger. The paper identifies material risks: sales volumes may be lower than forecast, total receipts may fall short, and Right to Buy sales are expected to decrease sharply as temporary discount levels end. Capital receipts of £35.297m are projected over four years.
findings.matters: Housing receipts are a key source of capital funding (£20.467m in 2026/27). Shortfalls would require alternative financing, borrowing increases, or reduction of other planned capital schemes.
findings.figures: Four-year capital receipts forecast: £35.297m (2026/27: £20.467m, 2027/28: £14.830m); Housing programmes: £240.505m (HRA) + £6.504m (GF)
findings.quote: There is a risk that the frequency of sales will be much slower than initial forecast when each housing development scheme was approved. There is also a risk that the total capital receipts will fall short of what was initially forecast.

daily_post.headline: Fund identified medium-level risk that inadequate cash could force below-market asset sales to meet pension payments
daily_post.lead: Liquidity pressure could force the Fund to crystallise losses by selling assets during market downturns, damaging long-term returns and potentially creating pressure for higher council contributions to recover funding levels.
